4	\section{Supplementary Material}
5	\label{sec:appendix}
6	
7	Unless noted otherwise, all analyses use OpenVLA-7B (\texttt{openvla/openvla-7b} on HuggingFace) evaluated on LIBERO-Goal (10 tasks $\times$ 50 demonstrations, $N = 63{,}228$ observations after excluding terminal frames).
8	Model conditions, representation extraction, metric definitions, and probe architectures follow \S\ref{sec:method}.
9	Cross-suite experiments (\S\ref{sec:cross_benchmark_appendix}) use LIBERO-Spatial with the same protocol (10 tasks $\times$ 50 demonstrations).
10	All experiments ran on 2$\times$ NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs (96\,GB each); random seed is 42 unless stated otherwise.
11	
12	\subsection{Architecture Summary}
13	Architecture details are provided in Table~\ref{tab:arch_overview} (main text).
14	
15	\subsection{OpenVLA-Specific Analysis Methods}
16	\label{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}
17	
18	Three additional analyses are applied to OpenVLA to characterize instruction encoding and representational geometry.
19	
20	\paragraph{Cross-instruction probes.}
21	Each visual frame is paired with all 10 LIBERO-Goal task instructions, producing 10 representation vectors per frame per layer.
22	A 10-way linear classifier identifies which instruction was present, applied separately at image\_mean and readout, with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) over 10 folds.
23	
24	\paragraph{Representational similarity analysis (RSA).}
25	RSA~\cite{kriegeskorte2008} quantifies geometric alignment between representations and the action space.
26	For each task, we compute pairwise representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) using cosine distances for representations and Euclidean distances for 7-D action vectors, from within-task observation pairs across 50 demonstrations.
27	Alignment is measured via Spearman $\rho$ between upper-triangular RDM entries; we report mean $\rho$ across 10 tasks with 95\% confidence intervals from 10{,}000 bootstrap resamples at the task level~\cite{nili2014toolbox}.
28	We prefer RSA over CKA~\cite{kornblith2019}: RSA captures relative distance structure via scale-invariant rank correlation, suited to comparing high- and low-dimensional spaces (4{,}096-D vs.\ 7-D), while CKA measures global subspace overlap that can remain high when geometric structure differs.
29	Both metrics are reported in \S\ref{sec:cka_appendix}; their divergence (\S\ref{sec:routing_synthesis}) confirms that neither alone fully characterizes representational structure.
30	
31	\paragraph{External baselines.}
32	DINOv2 ViT-L/14~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2} (\texttt{cls\_token}/\texttt{patch\_mean}) and CLIP ViT-L/14~\cite{radford2021_clip} (\texttt{patch\_mean}) provide self-supervised and vision-language pretrained reference points for probing and RSA.
33	
34	\subsection{OpenVLA Single-Architecture Deep Dive}
35	\label{sec:openvla_deepdive_appendix}
36	
37	This section provides the full single-architecture analysis summarized in \S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}.
38	
39	\paragraph{Cross-instruction probes.}
40	Cross-instruction probes validate the analysis framework on OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024_openvla}: as predicted by the causal mask, image\_mean instruction classification stays at chance ($10\%$) across all 32 layers in all conditions (full profile in \S\ref{sec:dense_routing}).
41	Trained readout achieves $100\%$ 10-way classification from L1 onward and maintains this through L31 (LOOCV-confirmed; \S\ref{sec:loocv}).
42	Reference readout also reaches $100\%$ at L1 but decays to $82\%$ by L31; the readout token is thus the primary multimodal integration site, and instruction encoding remains stable across depth in the trained model.
43	All patterns reproduce with a linear probe (\S\ref{sec:linear_probe}).
44	
45	\paragraph{L1 attention gradient.}
46	At L1, three conditions form a gradient of instruction attention: randomly initialized networks allocate 0/32 instruction-dominant heads ($11.7\%$ text attention, $1.5\times$ text-to-image ratio), Llama-2 base~\cite{touvron2023_llama2} allocates 9/32 ($36.5\%$), and VLA-trained allocates 24/32 ($57.7\%$, $38.2\times$ text-to-image ratio; \S\ref{sec:attention_decomp}).
47	The 32-layer attention profile reveals qualitatively distinct organizations: Llama-2 base concentrates instruction attention at mid-depth (L9--L16: 15--22 heads), while VLA fine-tuning produces an entry-exit bookend pattern with L0--L1 at 21--24 heads, L31 at 18, and intermediate layers at 0--11 (\S\ref{sec:threshold_sensitivity}).
48	Head counts are computed at a $50\%$ threshold; sensitivity analysis ($30\%$--$70\%$) confirms ordering robustness.
49	A fourth condition, OpenVLA fine-tuned on LIBERO, preserves L1 entry concentration (22/32 heads) but loses L31 exit re-engagement entirely (0 vs.\ 18 heads for the OXE-pretrained model), consistent with exit-layer attention serving multi-task flexibility rather than task-specific routing.
50	The redistribution beyond Llama-2 base priors is consistent with VLA fine-tuning being associated with instruction routing beyond what is inherited from language-model attention.
51	
52	\paragraph{Counterfactual perturbation.}
53	Four perturbation types across 10 LIBERO-Goal tasks produce large action divergence: wrong task ($d = 1.182$), empty instruction ($1.170$), shuffled tokens ($1.096$), paraphrased ($0.996$).
54	All four conditions yield $d \geq 1.0$, with ``wrong'' slightly exceeding ``empty.''
55	The effect replicates across LIBERO-Spatial (10 tasks): empty $1.173$, shuffled $0.979$, wrong $0.885$, paraphrased $0.807$ (Table~\ref{tab:counterfactual_spatial}).
56	Across both suites (20 tasks), the gradient spans $d = 0.81$--$1.18$.
57	Spatial instructions differ only in prepositions, yet wrong-task perturbation still produces $d = 0.885$; instruction-dominant heads route fine-grained spatial information, not merely task identity.
58	
59	\paragraph{Dose-response ablation.}
60	Dose-response ablation of L1 instruction-dominant heads produces monotonic trajectory divergence: $d$ rises from $0.482$ to $0.639$ as 4--32 heads are progressively ablated, with steep increase through 12 heads and plateau beyond 20 (\S\ref{sec:action_trajectory}).
61	Ablating all 24 instruction-dominant heads alters $72.3\%$ of action tokens (token-level $d = 0.65$, trajectory-level $d = 2.943$); control ablation of 8 random heads yields $d = 0.41$ ($29.3\%$ tokens affected), concentrated on the gripper dimension.
62	The routing effect is task-dependent: instruction-discriminative tasks show $2.5\times$ larger $|\Delta R^2|$ under L1 ablation than visually-sufficient tasks ($p = 0.033$; \S\ref{sec:task_complexity}).
63	
64	\paragraph{$R^2$ localization.}
65	$R^2$ action probing localizes training effects: trained readout peaks at $R^2 = 0.678$ (L13), reference readout peaks at $0.609$ (L32), and the training effect concentrates at the readout ($+0.069$) rather than at image\_mean ($+0.015$; \S\ref{sec:action_r2_threecond}).
66	These effects survive Bonferroni correction across all 63 tests (\S\ref{sec:bonferroni_correction}).
67

115	\paragraph{Metric constraints on trained--reference comparison.}
116	Trained models produce action outputs, enabling Cohen's $d$ on action MSE (OpenVLA, TraceVLA) or cosine distance on action tokens (NORA).
117	Reference VLMs (Phi-3-Vision, Qwen2.5-VL) do not generate actions; their sensitivity is measured via cosine distance on hidden representations---a metric with different scale, units, and distributional properties.
118	Ratios between Cohen's $d$ and cosine distance are therefore methodologically invalid, and we do not report cross-metric amplification factors.
119	Qualitatively, reference VLMs show weak sensitivity: the TraceVLA reference (Phi-3-Vision) produces peak cosine distances of $0.15$--$0.19$; the NORA reference (Qwen2.5-VL) yields $0.081$ on Goal.
120	
121	\paragraph{NORA details.}
122	NORA Goal produces saturated exit-layer cosine distances of $1.0$ for all conditions, with differentiation visible only at earlier layers (L24: wrong $= 0.123$, empty $= 0.098$).
123	NORA Spatial produces a peak cosine distance of $0.275$ for the ``wrong'' condition.

125	\subsection{CKA Analysis Method}
126	\label{sec:cka_appendix}
127	
128	We employ Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA)~\cite{kornblith2019} alongside RSA as a complementary perspective.
129	While RSA captures local geometric alignment via rank-order preservation, CKA measures global representational similarity through kernel-based comparisons.
130	
131	We compute both \emph{linear CKA}, which uses a linear kernel and is sensitive to second-order statistics, and \emph{RDM kernel CKA}, which operates on the same distance matrices as RSA but aggregates them differently.
132	Using both variants tests whether conclusions about representation structure are robust to the choice of similarity metric.
133	
134	Linear CKA between high-dimensional representations (4{,}096-D for LLM layers) and the 7-D action space is subject to a known dimension mismatch: the linear kernel in the low-dimensional space may not capture the same structure as in the high-dimensional space.
135	RDM kernel CKA avoids this issue by operating on distance matrices of equal size regardless of the original feature dimensionality.
136	
137	\subsection{Metric Sensitivity: RSA versus CKA}
138	Linear CKA~\cite{kornblith2019} reverses the RSA ordering: reference LLM ($\text{CKA} = 0.089$) $>$ trained LLM ($0.083$) $>$ DinoSigLIP+Projector ($0.081$) $>$ DINOv2 ($0.066$), partially inverting the self-supervised advantage (Figure~\ref{fig:metric_comparison}).
139	RDM kernel CKA partially resolves this discrepancy: trained ($0.260$) $\approx$ Projector ($0.257$) $>$ reference ($0.246$) $>$ DINOv2 ($0.241$).
140	This divergence reflects the known sensitivity of representation similarity metrics to different geometric properties.
141	
142	At the per-layer level, linear CKA between image\_mean and the action space rises monotonically from L0 ($0.081$) to L32 ($0.098$), with no inverted-U pattern.
143	RSA captures rank-order geometric alignment; CKA captures global linear structure.
144	The dissociation indicates that the geometric refinement in early layers operates on the relative arrangement of representations (affecting RSA) without altering the overall covariance structure (captured by CKA).
145	
146	\begin{figure}[t]
147	\centering

149	\caption{Three similarity metrics across representation sources. \textbf{(a)}~RSA ranks DINOv2 cls ($0.692$) $>$ Fused ($0.634$) $>$ Projector ($0.615$). \textbf{(b)}~Linear CKA reverses the ordering: Reference ($0.089$) $>$ Trained ($0.083$) $>$ Projector ($0.081$) $>$ DINOv2 ($0.066$). \textbf{(c)}~RDM kernel CKA: Trained ($0.260$) $\approx$ Projector ($0.257$) $>$ Reference ($0.246$) $>$ DINOv2 ($0.241$). The metric divergence underscores that RSA and CKA capture different aspects of representational structure.}
150	\label{fig:metric_comparison}
151	\end{figure}

153	\subsection{Branch-Split Detailed Analysis}
154	To disentangle the contributions of the two encoder streams within DinoSigLIP, we extract representations from the DINOv2 branch (1{,}024-D) and SigLIP branch (1{,}152-D) separately before fusion.
155	The two branches yield near-identical RSA: DINOv2 branch $\rho = 0.619$, SigLIP branch $\rho = 0.621$.
156	Fusion produces a representation ($\rho = 0.634$) that exceeds either branch alone; concatenation captures complementary structure.
157	The MLP projector then compresses this signal: DinoSigLIP+Projector achieves $\rho = 0.615$, a drop of $\Delta = 0.019$ from the fused 2{,}176-D input.
158	
159	\subsection{RSA Across Representation Sources}
160	Figure~\ref{fig:rsa_bar} shows RSA with the action space across all representation sources; the ordering matches the RSA results reported in \S\ref{sec:routing_synthesis}.

173	\subsection{Per-Layer Action Decoding Across Training Stages}
174	\label{sec:action_r2_threecond}
175	
176	Figure~\ref{fig:action_r2_threecond} compares per-layer action probe $R^2$ across three training stages (randomly initialized, Llama-2 base, VLA-trained) using 50 demonstrations per task, averaged over 3 seeds (mean $\pm$ std).
177	All three conditions share L0 representations ($R^2 = 0.645 \pm 0.008$); subsequent differences thus arise from Transformer processing rather than input variation.
178	The trained model peaks at L9 ($R^2 = 0.643 \pm 0.014$), consistent with progressive specialization for action-relevant feature integration.
179	Llama-2 base shows a steady decline (L0: $0.645 \to$ L32: $0.551$, std $0.003$--$0.035$), consistent with stable but unspecialized processing.
180	The randomly initialized model exhibits high cross-seed variance and deep-layer collapse, with negative $R^2$ and bimodal behavior across seeds at late layers; this instability indicates that randomly initialized Transformer layers produce destructive interference on action-relevant structure.
181	Random weights at intermediate layers produce anti-correlated representations ($R^2 < 0$, L10--L11), consistent with randomly initialized networks lacking structured computation.
182	The three-condition gradient (trained $>$ Llama-2 base $>$ randomly initialized) holds from L1 through L15, with a reversal at L32 where trained $R^2$ drops below the pretrained baseline.
183	The qualitative pattern is consistent across all 3 seeds.
184	Three conditions show substantial agreement in layer-wise $R^2$ ordering (Kendall's $W = 0.72$, $\chi^2 = 68.99$, $p < 0.001$).
185

188	\subsection{Random-Subset Ablation Details}
189	To evaluate whether the ablation effect in \S\ref{sec:openvla_routing} is specific to instruction-dominant heads, we compare dominant-head ablation against 30 random subsets of 24/32 L1 heads (each subset drawn without replacement).
190	Dominant-head ablation increases action $R^2$ by $+0.030$ (within-experiment baseline $0.524$), while random subsets yield a mean increase of $+0.071 \pm 0.013$ (Figure~\ref{fig:random_subset_ablation}).
191	The dominant-head effect falls below all 30 random subsets ($z = -3.11$, percentile $= 0\%$); heads with higher instruction-attention fraction carry more organized attention signals, consistent with graded rather than binary specialization.
192

196	\caption{$R^2$ increase from ablating 24/32 L1 heads. Gray bars: 30 random subsets; red line: dominant-24 heads ($+0.030$). Random subsets yield larger gains (mean $+0.071 \pm 0.013$; $z = -3.11$, percentile $= 0\%$), consistent with graded attention specialization across L1 heads.}
197	\label{fig:random_subset_ablation}
198	\end{figure}

200	\subsection{Action Trajectory Analysis Details}
201	\label{sec:action_trajectory}
202	
203	Table~\ref{tab:action_shift_perdim} reports per-dimension mean absolute shift for instruction-dominant (24 heads) and control (8 heads) L1 ablations.
204	Both conditions produce negligible shifts on translational dimensions ($dx$, $dy$, $dz$ $< 0.01$) and small rotational shifts ($rx$, $ry$, $rz$ $< 0.04$).
205	The gripper dimension absorbs the majority of the effect: instruction-head ablation shifts gripper predictions by $0.291$ (control: $0.141$), consistent with L1 attention influencing discrete open/close decisions.
206	
207	Per-task Cohen's $d$ values for instruction-head ablation are $0.43$, $0.69$, $0.70$, $0.70$, and $0.73$ (mean $0.65$), with all tasks significant ($p < 10^{-10}$).
208	Token-level KL divergence between original and ablated action distributions is $5.08$ for instruction heads and $1.69$ for control heads.
209	
210	\paragraph{Trajectory-level aggregation.}
211	Aggregating per-demo mean actions to the trajectory level reveals that token-level $d$ values are conservative: within-trajectory averaging reduces noise, yielding ${\sim}4\times$ larger effect sizes (mean token-to-trajectory ratio $0.245$).
212	Instruction-head ablation ($N = 50$: 5 tasks $\times$ 10 demos) yields trajectory $d = 2.943$ (95\% CI $[2.469, 3.707]$); bottom-24 non-instruction heads ($N = 30$) yield $d = 2.347$ (CI $[1.854, 3.221]$).
213	All 14 conditions produce trajectory $d > 2.0$ with CI lower bounds $> 1.7$.
214	Counterfactual trajectory-level $d$ (10 LIBERO-Goal tasks, $N = 100$): wrong $3.798$ (CI $[3.194, 4.938]$), empty $3.438$ ($[2.921, 4.448]$), shuffled $2.595$ ($[2.028, 3.791]$), paraphrased $2.131$ ($[1.740, 2.819]$).
215	Token-level $d$ underestimates trajectory-level effects by ${\times}3.1$--$4.5$, consistent with within-trajectory averaging reducing noise.
216	Fine-grained ordering is not reliably distinguished at trajectory level ($N = 100$); token-level comparisons ($N {\sim} 5{,}000$) provide higher resolution for ordering claims.
217	
218	\paragraph{Ground-truth action error.}
219	Ablation redirects model outputs ($d = 0.65$) but does not systematically increase error relative to expert demonstrations: original MSE $= 0.498$; top-24 instruction-head ablation MSE $= 0.497$ ($\Delta = -0.001$, Wilcoxon $p = 0.52$, n.s.); bottom-24 non-instruction heads MSE $= 0.506$ ($\Delta = +0.008$).
220	Changes concentrate on the gripper dimension; translation and rotation dimensions are negligibly affected.
221	Per-task breakdown shows all $|\Delta\text{MSE}| < 3\%$ of baseline with all $p > 0.27$; the near-zero aggregate $\Delta$ reflects uniformly small per-task effects rather than cancellation across tasks.
222	This is consistent with the information-computation dissociation: instruction-dominant heads control instruction-specific direction selection rather than action precision.
223	
224	Table~\ref{tab:perhead_bootstrap} reports per-head bootstrap CIs ($10{,}000$ resamples).
225	Individual control heads produce ${\sim}1.9\times$ stronger effects ($d = 0.051$) than instruction heads ($d = 0.027$, $p = 0.0018$), consistent across all 5 tasks.
226	The 24 instruction heads nonetheless produce a larger aggregate perturbation ($d = 0.65$ vs.\ $0.41$), consistent with collective coordination rather than individual strength.

304	\subsection{Pretrained LLM Representation Quality Under Visual Input}
305	A potential concern with the three-condition comparison (\S\ref{sec:arch_data}) is that the pretrained Llama-2 backbone never encountered projected visual tokens during pretraining, so its representations of such input could be degenerate.
306	We evaluate three diagnostics to assess representation quality.
307	Activation magnitude grows from $16.5$ (L0) to $90.2$ (L31) for Llama-2 base, compared to $16.5 \to 51.7$ for the VLA-trained model; the pretrained LLM produces larger but non-exploding activations with no evidence of collapse.

1050	\paragraph{Equivalence testing.}
1051	To formally test whether the cross-architecture peak $R^2$ values are statistically equivalent (rather than merely failing to differ), we apply the Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) procedure~\cite{lakens2017equivalence} with equivalence bound $\varepsilon = 0.05$.
1052	The observed difference is $\Delta = 0.003$ (OpenVLA L9: $0.637 \pm 0.008$; TraceVLA L11: $0.634 \pm 0.009$).
1053	Both one-sided tests reject at $p < 0.0001$; the 90\% confidence interval for the difference is $[-0.002, 0.009]$, falling entirely within $[-0.05, 0.05]$.
1054	A conventional two-sample $t$-test yields $p = 0.318$ (not significant), illustrating the distinction between absence of evidence for a difference and evidence of equivalence: the TOST procedure provides the latter.

1056	\subsection{Global Multiple Comparison Correction}
1057	\label{sec:bonferroni_correction}
1058	
1059	The paper reports 63 statistical tests spanning permutation tests, $t$-tests, bootstrap comparisons, TOST equivalence, and Spearman correlations.
1060	We apply a Bonferroni correction ($\alpha_{\text{adj}} = 0.05 / 63 = 7.94 \times 10^{-4}$) and the less conservative Holm--Bonferroni step-down procedure; both yield identical results.
1061	Of the 45 originally significant tests, 40 survive correction (88.9\%).
1062	
1063	All eight core tests supporting the paper's main claims remain significant:
1064	RSA permutation at L12 ($p < 0.0001$), trained vs.\ reference image geometry at L12 ($p = 3.9 \times 10^{-5}$), counterfactual wrong and empty instruction ($p < 10^{-100}$), TOST cross-architecture equivalence ($p < 0.0001$), dose-response top-24 ablation ($p < 10^{-100}$), trained vs.\ reference probe $R^2$ ($p < 0.0001$), and bottom-24 specificity ($p < 10^{-90}$).
1065	
1066	Five auxiliary tests lose significance under correction:
1067	(i)~RSA trained vs.\ reference preaction at L12 ($p = 0.005 \to p_{\text{adj}} = 0.284$),
1068	(ii)~DINOv2 vs.\ SigLIP RSA ($p = 0.032 \to p_{\text{adj}} = 1.0$),
1069	(iii)~fused backbone vs.\ SigLIP RSA ($p = 0.011 \to p_{\text{adj}} = 0.673$),
1070	(iv)~CV exact paired permutation ($p = 0.016 \to p_{\text{adj}} = 0.984$),
1071	and (v)~$R^2$ projector vs.\ VLA Spearman correlation ($p = 0.003 \to p_{\text{adj}} = 0.183$).
1072	These concern auxiliary comparisons (encoder ranking, coefficient-of-variation ordering) rather than the core redistribution, probing, or counterfactual findings; no main-text conclusion requires revision.
1073	
1074	\subsection{Mechanistic Interpretation}
1075	Matched-size ablation ($d$: instruction $0.65$, random $0.60$, image $0.58$; Table~\ref{tab:specificity_control}) and dose-response (steep through 12 heads, plateau beyond 20) indicate distributed attention redistribution.
1076	Counterfactual perturbation produces large effects across all conditions ($d = 1.0$--$1.2$ on Goal; \S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}), with shuffled tokens exceeding paraphrased ($d = 1.096$ vs.\ $0.996$) despite identical token sets, indicating positional sensitivity.
1077	That ablation raises $R^2$ yet alters trajectories ($d = 0.65$) without increasing ground-truth error ($\Delta\text{MSE} \approx 0$; \S\ref{sec:action_trajectory}) reflects an information-computation dissociation~\cite{hewitt2019control}: instruction-dominant heads control direction rather than precision. Random ablation yields larger $R^2$ gains ($+0.071$ vs.\ $+0.030$; $z = -3.11$, $0$\textsuperscript{th} percentile), consistent with distinct $R^2$ signatures.
1078	
1079	\subsection{Functional Stages and Predictions}
1080	Per-layer profiles suggest three stages: redistribution (L0--L1; probe $99.6\%$, 24/32 instruction-dominant heads), computation (L8--L13; $R^2$ peak $0.655$--$0.678$), and decay (L14--L31, ${\sim}56\%$ of parameters; declining $R^2$ and RSA suggest pruning potential).
1081	Task-specific fine-tuning eliminates L31 re-engagement (18 $\to$ 0 heads; \S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}), consistent with exit-layer attention serving multi-task flexibility ($N{=}2$).
1082	TraceVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla} (Phi-3-V) shows consistent entry-exit attention concentration from an opposite starting point (\S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}).
1083	The $2 {\times} 2$ trained-vs-reference comparison reveals a consistent reorganization pattern: reference OpenVLA collapses from L0 ($R^2 = 0.629$) to near-zero at mid-layers (L20: $0.086$, std $= 0.277$), while reference Phi-3-V peaks at L6 ($0.578$) with gradual decline (std $= 0.068$)---qualitatively opposite reference landscapes.
1084	Yet training drives both to nearly identical mid-layer peaks ($0.637$ vs.\ $0.634$, $\Delta = 0.003$) with stabilized deep-layer variance (OpenVLA std $0.277 \to 0.040$; Phi-3-V $0.068 \to 0.011$).
1085	This consistent outcome from divergent starting points suggests that mid-layer action specialization is a consistent convergence pattern of VLA training, not an architectural artifact.
1086	Exit-layer $R^2$ differs ($0.488$ vs.\ $0.557$), possibly reflecting architectural differences in late-layer processing.
1087	Remaining predictions: cross-attention VLAs ($\pi_0$~\cite{black2024_pi0}, Octo~\cite{ghosh2024_octo}) should lack L1 instruction-dominant heads; larger VLAs should yield flatter per-head contributions.
1088	For deployments, L1 instruction probes can flag instruction-discriminative tasks and L1 attention entropy can monitor instruction under-attendance at runtime.

1090	\subsection{Extended Discussion}
1091	\label{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}
1092	
1093	\paragraph{Observational three-tier gradient.}
1094	The cross-architecture matrix suggests a three-tier gradient of representational adaptation.
1095	Tier~1 (VLM bases, no action training): inherited L1 attention (TraceVLA 32/32, NORA 13--14/16), negligible exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 \leq 0.048$), and minimal counterfactual sensitivity (cosine distance $\leq 0.185$).
1096	Tier~2 (general-purpose VLA, OXE-pretrained): strong L1 routing (24--26/32 heads), moderate counterfactual sensitivity ($d \approx 1.0$), and no systematic exit collapse across suites.
1097	Tier~3 (task-specific VLAs, fine-tuned on LIBERO): exit collapse at every VLM-to-VLA cell and medium-to-large counterfactual sensitivity ($d = 0.45$--$1.52$).
1098	This gradient is suggestive but limited: Tier~2 contains a single architecture (OpenVLA), and the Tier~2/Tier~3 boundary confounds training stage with architecture.
1099	Testing additional general-purpose VLAs (e.g., Octo~\cite{ghosh2024_octo}, $\pi_0$~\cite{black2024_pi0}) at Tier~2 is necessary before the three-tier structure can be treated as a robust empirical pattern.
1100	
1101	\paragraph{Exit collapse mechanism.}
1102	One possible explanation for the VLM-to-VLA / VLA-to-VLA asymmetry is that VLM-to-VLA references lack action-relevant exit-layer structure, forcing mid-layer construction without exit preservation (analogous to fine-tuning-induced feature distortion~\cite{kumar2022finetuning}), while VLA-to-VLA references already maintain this structure.
1103	Validating this explanation causally requires controlled training-stage experiments, but the consistency across architectures supports its directional value.
1104	
1105	\paragraph{Behavioral relevance.}
1106	Correlating trained $\Delta R^2$ with published LIBERO success rates across all nine available architecture-suite cells yields a positive but non-significant trend (Spearman $\rho = 0.583$, $p = 0.10$, $n = 9$), marginally above the conventional significance threshold.
1107	Within-suite comparisons, which control for task difficulty, are uniformly positive: on Goal ($n = 3$ architectures), $\Delta R^2$ and success rate are perfectly rank-correlated ($\rho = 1.0$), and every remaining suite ($n = 2$ each) shows the same direction.
1108	This directional evidence is consistent with stronger mid-network action encoding (higher peak $R^2$) followed by more aggressive exit-layer compression being associated with better task performance.
1109	Several caveats temper this interpretation: architecture capacity differences (model size, backbone quality) are not controlled, suite difficulty co-varies with both $\Delta R^2$ and success rate, multiple suites from the same architecture are not independent observations, and the sample size limits statistical power.
1110	Post-hoc power analysis (Fisher $Z$-transform, two-tailed $\alpha = 0.05$) yields achieved power $= 0.37$ at $n = 9$; reaching $80\%$ power would require $n \geq 21$ architecture-suite cells.
1111	The current analysis is therefore underpowered, and the non-significant $p$-value should not be interpreted as evidence of absence; it reflects insufficient sample size rather than a weak effect.
1112	This correlational evidence does not establish a causal link between exit collapse and task success.
1113	Closed-loop behavioral validation, including intervention experiments that directly manipulate exit-layer representations, remains a priority for future work.
1114	
1115	\paragraph{Closed-loop evaluation attempt.}
1116	We attempted closed-loop evaluation on LIBERO-Goal using the OpenVLA official checkpoint but achieved SR$=$0/3 across tested configurations, consistent with known reproducibility challenges in VLA deployment (sensitivity to hardware setup, action tokenization, and environment configuration).
1117	This negative result motivates our representational analysis approach, which does not require successful task completion.
1118	
1119	\paragraph{Metric constraints.}
1120	Counterfactual sensitivity is measured via Cohen's $d$ on action MSE for models that produce actions and via cosine distance on hidden representations for reference VLMs (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).
1121	These metrics differ in scale and distributional properties; ratios between them are not meaningful.
1122	The OpenVLA Long-Horizon inversion (trained $d = 0.56$, reference $d = 1.05$) illustrates how same-metric comparisons can reverse the expected direction, cautioning against overinterpretation of any single cell.
1123	A standardized metric framework for cross-condition counterfactual comparison remains an open problem.
1124	
1125	\paragraph{Extended limitations.}
1126	Each architecture is analyzed at a single trained checkpoint, precluding characterization of how exit collapse or counterfactual sensitivity develop during training.
1127	All analyses are open-loop, consistent with prior representational studies~\cite{grant2026,haon2025}; closed-loop validation would provide complementary evidence about the behavioral relevance of the identified routing structures.
1128	The three-tier gradient has $n = 1$ at Tier~2, limiting its inferential power; populating this tier with additional general-purpose VLAs is a priority for future work.
1129	
1130	\paragraph{Coarse training dynamics.}
1131	Although intermediate checkpoints are unavailable (\S\ref{sec:limitations}), the cross-condition design provides coarse-grained evidence about when exit collapse emerges.
1132	Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics} plots $\Delta R^2$ across four training-pathway categories.
1133	NLP fine-tuning ($\Delta R^2 = 0.000$) and pretrained references ($\Delta R^2 \leq 0.097$) cluster below the $0.10$ threshold; VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning produces large collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.156$--$0.455$); subsequent VLA-to-VLA fine-tuning does not intensify it ($\Delta R^2 = 0.033$--$0.086$).
1134	This constrains the onset: exit collapse emerges during the first action-grounded training stage and does not accumulate with continued task-specific fine-tuning.

1143	\subsection{Extended Practical Implications}
1144	\label{sec:extended_practical_implications}
1145	
1146	The main text identifies three use cases for the entry-exit decomposition; here we elaborate on each.
1147	
1148	\paragraph{Checkpoint selection.}
1149	$\Delta R^2$ provides a probe-based screening signal ($> 0.10$ flags reorganization) requiring only a forward pass and a linear probe.
1150	Its wall-clock cost scales with model size rather than environment complexity, unlike rollout evaluation which requires physics simulation and multi-step execution.
1151	Practitioners can rank checkpoints by $\Delta R^2$ and reserve rollout budgets for the top candidates, substantially reducing the number of expensive closed-loop evaluations needed during model selection.
1152	
1153	\paragraph{Transfer learning strategy.}
1154	The flat VLA-to-VLA $\Delta R^2$ profile (\S\ref{sec:r2_collapse}) shows that VLA-to-VLA transitions preserve exit structure, justifying staged pipelines (VLM$\to$VLA$\to$task) that reuse the first-stage action head without re-learning exit representations.
1155	Inherited L1 routing can further serve as a frozen prior, reducing tunable parameters during domain transfer.
1156	This suggests that practitioners adapting a general-purpose VLA to a new task suite may benefit from freezing early layers while focusing capacity on mid-to-late layer adaptation.
1157	
1158	\paragraph{Mid-layer probe value.}
1159	Where exit collapse is pronounced, mid-layer representations ($R^2$ peak at L9--L11 across architectures) outperform exit-layer features for downstream tasks such as reward modeling, distillation targets, or auxiliary prediction heads.
1160	For knowledge distillation, matching mid-layer features of the teacher rather than exit-layer features may yield better student performance in VLA settings.
1161	For reward modeling, training reward predictors on mid-layer features rather than final-layer outputs may provide more informative training signals.

\paragraph{Equivalence testing.}
To formally test whether the cross-architecture peak $R^2$ values are statistically equivalent (rather than merely failing to differ), we apply the Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) procedure~\cite{lakens2017equivalence} with equivalence bound $\varepsilon = 0.05$.
The observed difference is $\Delta = 0.003$ (OpenVLA L9: $0.637 \pm 0.008$; TraceVLA L11: $0.634 \pm 0.009$).
Both one-sided tests reject at $p < 0.0001$; the 90\% confidence interval for the difference is $[-0.002, 0.009]$, falling entirely within $[-0.05, 0.05]$.
A conventional two-sample $t$-test yields $p = 0.318$ (not significant), illustrating the distinction between absence of evidence for a difference and evidence of equivalence: the TOST procedure provides the latter.

\subsection{Global Multiple Comparison Correction}
\label{sec:bonferroni_correction}

The paper reports 63 statistical tests spanning permutation tests, $t$-tests, bootstrap comparisons, TOST equivalence, and Spearman correlations.
We apply a Bonferroni correction ($\alpha_{\text{adj}} = 0.05 / 63 = 7.94 \times 10^{-4}$) and the less conservative Holm--Bonferroni step-down procedure; both yield identical results.
Of the 45 originally significant tests, 40 survive correction (88.9\%).

All eight core tests supporting the paper's main claims remain significant:
RSA permutation at L12 ($p < 0.0001$), trained vs.\ reference image geometry at L12 ($p = 3.9 \times 10^{-5}$), counterfactual wrong and empty instruction ($p < 10^{-100}$), TOST cross-architecture equivalence ($p < 0.0001$), dose-response top-24 ablation ($p < 10^{-100}$), trained vs.\ reference probe $R^2$ ($p < 0.0001$), and bottom-24 specificity ($p < 10^{-90}$).

Five auxiliary tests lose significance under correction:
(i)~RSA trained vs.\ reference preaction at L12 ($p = 0.005 \to p_{\text{adj}} = 0.284$),
(ii)~DINOv2 vs.\ SigLIP RSA ($p = 0.032 \to p_{\text{adj}} = 1.0$),
(iii)~fused backbone vs.\ SigLIP RSA ($p = 0.011 \to p_{\text{adj}} = 0.673$),
(iv)~CV exact paired permutation ($p = 0.016 \to p_{\text{adj}} = 0.984$),
and (v)~$R^2$ projector vs.\ VLA Spearman correlation ($p = 0.003 \to p_{\text{adj}} = 0.183$).
These concern auxiliary comparisons (encoder ranking, coefficient-of-variation ordering) rather than the core redistribution, probing, or counterfactual findings; no main-text conclusion requires revision.

\subsection{Mechanistic Interpretation}
Matched-size ablation ($d$: instruction $0.65$, random $0.60$, image $0.58$; Table~\ref{tab:specificity_control}) and dose-response (steep through 12 heads, plateau beyond 20) indicate distributed attention redistribution.
Counterfactual perturbation produces large effects across all conditions ($d = 1.0$--$1.2$ on Goal; \S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}), with shuffled tokens exceeding paraphrased ($d = 1.096$ vs.\ $0.996$) despite identical token sets, indicating positional sensitivity.
That ablation raises $R^2$ yet alters trajectories ($d = 0.65$) without increasing ground-truth error ($\Delta\text{MSE} \approx 0$; \S\ref{sec:action_trajectory}) reflects an information-computation dissociation~\cite{hewitt2019control}: instruction-dominant heads control direction rather than precision. Random ablation yields larger $R^2$ gains ($+0.071$ vs.\ $+0.030$; $z = -3.11$, $0$\textsuperscript{th} percentile), consistent with distinct $R^2$ signatures.

\subsection{Functional Stages and Predictions}
Per-layer profiles suggest three stages: redistribution (L0--L1; probe $99.6\%$, 24/32 instruction-dominant heads), computation (L8--L13; $R^2$ peak $0.655$--$0.678$), and decay (L14--L31, ${\sim}56\%$ of parameters; declining $R^2$ and RSA suggest pruning potential).
Task-specific fine-tuning eliminates L31 re-engagement (18 $\to$ 0 heads; \S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}), consistent with exit-layer attention serving multi-task flexibility ($N{=}2$).
TraceVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla} (Phi-3-V) shows consistent entry-exit attention concentration from an opposite starting point (\S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}).
The $2 {\times} 2$ trained-vs-reference comparison reveals a consistent reorganization pattern: reference OpenVLA collapses from L0 ($R^2 = 0.629$) to near-zero at mid-layers (L20: $0.086$, std $= 0.277$), while reference Phi-3-V peaks at L6 ($0.578$) with gradual decline (std $= 0.068$)---qualitatively opposite reference landscapes.
Yet training drives both to nearly identical mid-layer peaks ($0.637$ vs.\ $0.634$, $\Delta = 0.003$) with stabilized deep-layer variance (OpenVLA std $0.277 \to 0.040$; Phi-3-V $0.068 \to 0.011$).
This consistent outcome from divergent starting points suggests that mid-layer action specialization is a consistent convergence pattern of VLA training, not an architectural artifact.
Exit-layer $R^2$ differs ($0.488$ vs.\ $0.557$), possibly reflecting architectural differences in late-layer processing.
Remaining predictions: cross-attention VLAs ($\pi_0$~\cite{black2024_pi0}, Octo~\cite{ghosh2024_octo}) should lack L1 instruction-dominant heads; larger VLAs should yield flatter per-head contributions.
For deployments, L1 instruction probes can flag instruction-discriminative tasks and L1 attention entropy can monitor instruction under-attendance at runtime.

\subsection{Extended Discussion}
\label{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}

\paragraph{Observational three-tier gradient.}
The cross-architecture matrix suggests a three-tier gradient of representational adaptation.
Tier~1 (VLM bases, no action training): inherited L1 attention (TraceVLA 32/32, NORA 13--14/16), negligible exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 \leq 0.048$), and minimal counterfactual sensitivity (cosine distance $\leq 0.185$).
Tier~2 (general-purpose VLA, OXE-pretrained): strong L1 routing (24--26/32 heads), moderate counterfactual sensitivity ($d \approx 1.0$), and no systematic exit collapse across suites.
Tier~3 (task-specific VLAs, fine-tuned on LIBERO): exit collapse at every VLM-to-VLA cell and medium-to-large counterfactual sensitivity ($d = 0.45$--$1.52$).
This gradient is suggestive but limited: Tier~2 contains a single architecture (OpenVLA), and the Tier~2/Tier~3 boundary confounds training stage with architecture.
Testing additional general-purpose VLAs (e.g., Octo~\cite{ghosh2024_octo}, $\pi_0$~\cite{black2024_pi0}) at Tier~2 is necessary before the three-tier structure can be treated as a robust empirical pattern.

\paragraph{Exit collapse mechanism.}
One possible explanation for the VLM-to-VLA / VLA-to-VLA asymmetry is that VLM-to-VLA references lack action-relevant exit-layer structure, forcing mid-layer construction without exit preservation (analogous to fine-tuning-induced feature distortion~\cite{kumar2022finetuning}), while VLA-to-VLA references already maintain this structure.
Validating this explanation causally requires controlled training-stage experiments, but the consistency across architectures supports its directional value.

\paragraph{Behavioral relevance.}
Correlating trained $\Delta R^2$ with published LIBERO success rates across all nine available architecture-suite cells yields a positive but non-significant trend (Spearman $\rho = 0.583$, $p = 0.10$, $n = 9$), marginally above the conventional significance threshold.
Within-suite comparisons, which control for task difficulty, are uniformly positive: on Goal ($n = 3$ architectures), $\Delta R^2$ and success rate are perfectly rank-correlated ($\rho = 1.0$), and every remaining suite ($n = 2$ each) shows the same direction.
This directional evidence is consistent with stronger mid-network action encoding (higher peak $R^2$) followed by more aggressive exit-layer compression being associated with better task performance.
Several caveats temper this interpretation: architecture capacity differences (model size, backbone quality) are not controlled, suite difficulty co-varies with both $\Delta R^2$ and success rate, multiple suites from the same architecture are not independent observations, and the sample size limits statistical power.
Post-hoc power analysis (Fisher $Z$-transform, two-tailed $\alpha = 0.05$) yields achieved power $= 0.37$ at $n = 9$; reaching $80\%$ power would require $n \geq 21$ architecture-suite cells.
The current analysis is therefore underpowered, and the non-significant $p$-value should not be interpreted as evidence of absence; it reflects insufficient sample size rather than a weak effect.
This correlational evidence does not establish a causal link between exit collapse and task success.
Closed-loop behavioral validation, including intervention experiments that directly manipulate exit-layer representations, remains a priority for future work.

\paragraph{Closed-loop evaluation attempt.}
We attempted closed-loop evaluation on LIBERO-Goal using the OpenVLA official checkpoint but achieved SR$=$0/3 across tested configurations, consistent with known reproducibility challenges in VLA deployment (sensitivity to hardware setup, action tokenization, and environment configuration).
This negative result motivates our representational analysis approach, which does not require successful task completion.

\paragraph{Metric constraints.}
Counterfactual sensitivity is measured via Cohen's $d$ on action MSE for models that produce actions and via cosine distance on hidden representations for reference VLMs (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).
These metrics differ in scale and distributional properties; ratios between them are not meaningful.
The OpenVLA Long-Horizon inversion (trained $d = 0.56$, reference $d = 1.05$) illustrates how same-metric comparisons can reverse the expected direction, cautioning against overinterpretation of any single cell.
A standardized metric framework for cross-condition counterfactual comparison remains an open problem.

\paragraph{Extended limitations.}
Each architecture is analyzed at a single trained checkpoint, precluding characterization of how exit collapse or counterfactual sensitivity develop during training.
All analyses are open-loop, consistent with prior representational studies~\cite{grant2026,haon2025}; closed-loop validation would provide complementary evidence about the behavioral relevance of the identified routing structures.
The three-tier gradient has $n = 1$ at Tier~2, limiting its inferential power; populating this tier with additional general-purpose VLAs is a priority for future work.

\paragraph{Coarse training dynamics.}
Although intermediate checkpoints are unavailable (\S\ref{sec:limitations}), the cross-condition design provides coarse-grained evidence about when exit collapse emerges.
Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics} plots $\Delta R^2$ across four training-pathway categories.
NLP fine-tuning ($\Delta R^2 = 0.000$) and pretrained references ($\Delta R^2 \leq 0.097$) cluster below the $0.10$ threshold; VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning produces large collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.156$--$0.455$); subsequent VLA-to-VLA fine-tuning does not intensify it ($\Delta R^2 = 0.033$--$0.086$).
This constrains the onset: exit collapse emerges during the first action-grounded training stage and does not accumulate with continued task-specific fine-tuning.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.55\columnwidth]{figures/fig_training_dynamics.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{$\Delta R^2$ across training pathways.} Each point is one architecture-suite cell; markers distinguish backbone families. Exit collapse (above dashed line) is confined to VLM-to-VLA transitions and does not intensify during VLA-to-VLA fine-tuning.}
\label{fig:training_dynamics}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Extended Practical Implications}
\label{sec:extended_practical_implications}

The main text identifies three use cases for the entry-exit decomposition; here we elaborate on each.

\paragraph{Checkpoint selection.}
$\Delta R^2$ provides a probe-based screening signal ($> 0.10$ flags reorganization) requiring only a forward pass and a linear probe.
Its wall-clock cost scales with model size rather than environment complexity, unlike rollout evaluation which requires physics simulation and multi-step execution.
Practitioners can rank checkpoints by $\Delta R^2$ and reserve rollout budgets for the top candidates, substantially reducing the number of expensive closed-loop evaluations needed during model selection.

\paragraph{Transfer learning strategy.}
The flat VLA-to-VLA $\Delta R^2$ profile (\S\ref{sec:r2_collapse}) shows that VLA-to-VLA transitions preserve exit structure, justifying staged pipelines (VLM$\to$VLA$\to$task) that reuse the first-stage action head without re-learning exit representations.
Inherited L1 routing can further serve as a frozen prior, reducing tunable parameters during domain transfer.
This suggests that practitioners adapting a general-purpose VLA to a new task suite may benefit from freezing early layers while focusing capacity on mid-to-late layer adaptation.

\paragraph{Mid-layer probe value.}
Where exit collapse is pronounced, mid-layer representations ($R^2$ peak at L9--L11 across architectures) outperform exit-layer features for downstream tasks such as reward modeling, distillation targets, or auxiliary prediction heads.
For knowledge distillation, matching mid-layer features of the teacher rather than exit-layer features may yield better student performance in VLA settings.
For reward modeling, training reward predictors on mid-layer features rather than final-layer outputs may provide more informative training signals.

\subsection{Methodological Context}
Representational analysis is an established methodology in the interpretability tradition; behavioral validation provides complementary evidence but is not a prerequisite for mechanistic characterization.
Table~\ref{tab:methodological_precedent} situates our approach within this tradition.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{\textbf{Methodological precedent.} Representative interpretability studies and their use of behavioral evaluation. Partial behavioral eval includes correlational or indirect evidence.}
\label{tab:methodological_precedent}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Paper} & \textbf{Domain} & \textbf{Method} & \textbf{Behav.\ eval?} \\
\midrule
Belinkov~\cite{belinkov2022} & NLP & Probing survey & No \\
Olsson et al.~\cite{olsson2022} & LM & Induction heads & No \\
Wang et al.~\cite{wang2023_ioi} & LM & IOI circuit & No \\
Meng et al.~\cite{meng2022_rome} & LM & Causal tracing (localization) & No \\
Grant et al.~\cite{grant2026} & VLA & Visual dominance & Partial \\
Haon et al.~\cite{haon2025} & VLA & Sparse directions & No \\
\midrule
Ours & VLA & $\Delta R^2$ + attn.\ profiling & Partial ($\rho{=}0.583$) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{NLP Finetuning Controls}
\label{sec:nlp_control_appendix}

Table~\ref{tab:nlp_controls} compares the three NLP finetuning controls used to test whether exit collapse is specific to action-oriented training.
All three chat-finetuned models produce flat action-probe profiles with $\Delta R^2 = 0.000$, confirming that NLP instruction tuning does not induce the peak-to-exit drop observed in VLM-to-VLA transitions in any of the three backbone families.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{\textbf{NLP finetuning control comparison.} All three models are instruction-tuned for conversational use without action heads or robot demonstration data. None exhibits exit collapse.}
\label{tab:nlp_controls}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{VLA backbone} & \textbf{$\Delta R^2$} & \textbf{Mean $R^2$} & \textbf{Layers} \\
\midrule
Llama-2-7b-chat & OpenVLA (Llama-2-7B) & 0.000 & $0.155 \pm 0.001$ & 32 \\
Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct & TraceVLA (Phi-3-mini) & 0.000 & $0.155 \pm 0.000$ & 32 \\
Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct$^{*}$ & NORA (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) & 0.000 & $0.155 \pm 0.000$ & 36 \\
\bottomrule
\multicolumn{5}{l}{\footnotesize $^{*}$Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct shares the Qwen2.5 language backbone with NORA's}\\
\multicolumn{5}{l}{\footnotesize Qwen2.5-VL-3B but lacks the vision encoder and cross-attention modules.}\\
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Figure~\ref{fig:r2_collapse} (main text) overlays the NLP control profiles (dotted gray) against the corresponding VLA trained and reference curves.

\subsection{Claim-Evidence Summary}
\label{sec:claim_evidence_appendix}

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_claim_evidence.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{Claim--evidence--scope summary.} Each main finding is paired with its supporting analysis and its main limitation. The figure distinguishes directly observed representational patterns from stronger causal interpretations that require interventional or training-dynamics evidence.}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Cross-Architecture Design Rationale}
The two VLM-to-VLA transitions (TraceVLA and NORA) were selected to maximize structural diversity within the constraint of publicly available LIBERO-evaluated checkpoints.
Table~\ref{tab:arch_diversity} summarizes the design-axis differences.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{\textbf{Structural diversity between the two VLM-to-VLA transitions.} The two architectures differ on nearly every major design axis, strengthening the generality of shared findings.}
\label{tab:arch_diversity}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Design Axis} & \textbf{TraceVLA} & \textbf{NORA} \\
\midrule
Language backbone & Phi-3-mini (3.8B) & Qwen2.5-VL (3B) \\
Backbone family & Microsoft & Alibaba \\
Attention mechanism & Multi-Head Attention & Grouped-Query Attention \\
Number of layers & 32 & 36 \\
Vision encoder & SigLIP (shared w/ base) & Native ViT (dynamic resolution) \\
Vision integration & Projector (late fusion) & Token concatenation (native) \\
Pretraining data & English-centric web & Multilingual web + code \\
Action head design & Linear projection & MLP \\
Training data & OXE + LIBERO & OXE + LIBERO + custom \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Despite these differences, both transitions exhibit the same exit-collapse pattern ($\Delta R^2 = 0.156$--$0.455$), while their respective reference VLMs show only small fluctuations ($\Delta R^2 \leq 0.097$).
The probability of observing consistent collapse in two structurally divergent architectures under a null hypothesis of random association is low (permutation test $p = 0.008$; \S\ref{sec:delta_r2_threshold}).
Structural diversity thus provides evidential weight beyond what the raw $N = 2$ count suggests.

\subsection{Convergent Evidence Summary}
Three methodologically distinct approaches triangulate instruction routing in VLAs.
Table~\ref{tab:convergent_evidence} summarizes what each method measures, its key finding, evidence type, and acknowledged limitation.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{\textbf{Convergent evidence across three analytical methods.} Each method addresses a different aspect of instruction routing; no single method is sufficient alone, but their convergence strengthens the overall characterization.}
\label{tab:convergent_evidence}
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{2.0cm}p{2.8cm}p{3.2cm}p{1.8cm}p{2.8cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{What it measures} & \textbf{Key finding} & \textbf{Evidence type} & \textbf{Limitation} \\
\midrule
Layer-wise probing (\S\ref{sec:r2_collapse}) & Where action-relevant information is decodable & VLM-to-VLA: peak-to-exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.16$--$0.46$); VLA-to-VLA: flat & Correlational (decodability) & Does not establish causal necessity \\
\addlinespace
Counterfactual perturbation (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}) & Whether instruction content affects model outputs & All trained VLAs: graded divergence ($d = 0.45$--$1.52$) ordered by perturbation severity & Behavioral (input--output) & Does not localize which layers are responsible \\
\addlinespace
Attention head ablation (Appendix~\ref{sec:action_trajectory}) & Whether identified structures carry functional signals & Dose-response: monotonic divergence ($d = 0.48$--$0.64$) upon progressive head removal & Interventional (causal contribution) & Single architecture (OpenVLA); contribution $\neq$ necessity \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The three methods form a complementary chain: probing identifies \emph{where} instruction information concentrates across layers, perturbation confirms \emph{whether} instruction content functionally affects behavior, and ablation demonstrates \emph{that} the identified attention structures carry relevant signals.
No method alone supports causal claims about instruction routing mechanisms; their convergence provides stronger evidence than any single approach.

\section{Use of Generative AI}
\label{sec:use_of_ai}

Generative AI tools (Claude, GPT-4) assisted with code implementation and manuscript editing; all scientific content was produced by the authors.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    'font.family': 'serif',
    'font.serif': ['Liberation Serif'],
    'pdf.fonttype': 42,
    'ps.fonttype': 42,
    'mathtext.fontset': 'custom',
    'mathtext.rm': 'Liberation Serif',
    'mathtext.it': 'Liberation Serif:italic',
    'mathtext.bf': 'Liberation Serif:bold',
})
import numpy as np
import os

COLORS = {
    'empty': '#F4C28C',
    'wrong': '#9DC4E6',
    'shuffled': '#A3D4A8',
    'paraphrased': '#D4AACC',
}
EDGE = {
    'empty': '#D9A56C',
    'wrong': '#7AA4C8',
    'shuffled': '#7CB888',
    'paraphrased': '#B88EAE',
}

conditions = ['empty', 'wrong', 'shuffled', 'paraphrased']
cond_labels = ['E', 'W', 'S', 'P']
n_cond = len(conditions)

# ── Panel A data: Cohen's d ──
cohens_d = {
    'OV-G': [1.17, 1.18, 1.10, 1.00],
    'OV-S': [1.17, 0.89, 0.98, 0.81],
    'OV-O': [1.21, 1.19, 1.12, 0.90],
    'OV-L': [0.51, 0.55, 0.57, 0.45],
    'TV-G': [1.52, 1.40, 1.34, 1.21],
    'TV-S': [1.33, 1.17, 1.30, 1.18],
    'TV-O': [1.21, 1.06, 1.16, 0.97],
    'TV-L': [1.47, 1.42, 1.39, 1.16],
}

# ── Panel B data: Cosine distance ──
cosine_dist = {
    'G':    [1.0,    1.0,    1.0,    1.0],
    'S':    [0.24,   0.275,  0.12,   0.03],
    'G.':   [0.1530, 0.0160, 0.0839, 0.0043],
    'S.':   [0.1805, 0.0046, 0.1395, 0.0044],
    'O':    [0.1850, 0.0044, 0.0977, 0.0052],
    'L':    [0.1734, 0.0221, 0.1204, 0.0070],
    'G..':  [0.0814, 0.0143, 0.0332, 0.0041],
    'S..':  [0.0807, 0.0020, 0.0313, 0.0047],
}
panelB_display = ['G', 'S', 'G', 'S', 'O', 'L', 'G', 'S']
panelB_regions = [
    ('NORA\n(trained)', 0, 2),
    ('Phi-3-Vision\n(ref)', 2, 6),
    ('Qwen2.5-VL\n(ref)', 6, 8),
]

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.0, 3.0),
                                gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [1.1, 1]})

# ── Panel A ──
bar_w = 0.20
groups_a = list(cohens_d.keys())
n_a = len(groups_a)
boundary = 4

positions_a = np.zeros(n_a)
gap = 0.6
for i in range(n_a):
    positions_a[i] = float(i) + (gap if i >= boundary else 0)

for j, cond in enumerate(conditions):
    offset = (j - (n_cond - 1) / 2) * bar_w
    vals = [cohens_d[g][j] for g in groups_a]
    ax1.bar(positions_a + offset, vals, bar_w,
            color=COLORS[cond], edgecolor=EDGE[cond], linewidth=0.8,
            label=cond_labels[j], zorder=3)

ax1.axhline(y=0.8, color='gray', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5, linewidth=1, zorder=1)
ax1.text(positions_a[-1] + 0.3, 0.82, 'large effect', fontsize=8, color='gray',
         alpha=0.7, va='bottom', ha='left')

sep_x = (positions_a[boundary - 1] + positions_a[boundary]) / 2
ax1.axvline(x=sep_x, color='gray', linestyle=':', alpha=0.4, linewidth=1)

ax1.set_xticks(positions_a)
ax1.set_xticklabels(groups_a, fontsize=9, rotation=45, ha='right')
ax1.set_ylabel("Cohen's d", fontsize=10)
ax1.set_ylim(0, 1.8)
ax1.set_title("(a) Cohen's d: OpenVLA & TraceVLA", fontsize=11, fontweight='bold', loc='left')
ax1.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax1.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax1.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=9)
ax1.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.2, linewidth=0.5)
ax1.legend(loc='upper right', ncol=4, fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9,
           edgecolor='gray', handlelength=0.8, handletextpad=0.2, columnspacing=0.4)

# ── Panel B ──
bar_w_b = 0.18
groups_b = list(cosine_dist.keys())
n_b = len(groups_b)

positions_b = np.zeros(n_b)
region_gap = 0.9
pos = 0.0
for i in range(n_b):
    if i == 2 or i == 6:
        pos += region_gap
    positions_b[i] = pos
    pos += 1.0

ylim_b = (0, 0.35)
sat_cap = ylim_b[1] * 0.85

for j, cond in enumerate(conditions):
    offset = (j - (n_cond - 1) / 2) * bar_w_b
    vals = [cosine_dist[g][j] for g in groups_b]
    bars = ax2.bar(positions_b + offset, vals, bar_w_b,
                   color=COLORS[cond], edgecolor=EDGE[cond], linewidth=0.8,
                   label=cond_labels[j] if j < 4 else None, zorder=3)
    for k, (bar, v) in enumerate(zip(bars, vals)):
        if v >= 0.95:
            bar.set_height(sat_cap)
            if j == 0:
                ax2.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2 + bar_w_b * 0.8,
                         sat_cap + 0.005, '1.0\n(sat.)', ha='center', va='bottom',
                         fontsize=6.5, fontweight='bold', color='#333333')

for rname, rstart, rend in panelB_regions:
    if rstart > 0:
        sx = (positions_b[rstart - 1] + positions_b[rstart]) / 2
        ax2.axvline(x=sx, color='gray', linestyle=':', alpha=0.5, linewidth=1)

for rname, rstart, rend in panelB_regions:
    center = (positions_b[rstart] + positions_b[rend - 1]) / 2
    ax2.text(center, -0.15, rname, ha='center', va='top', fontsize=8,
             fontweight='bold', transform=ax2.get_xaxis_transform())

ax2.set_xticks(positions_b)
ax2.set_xticklabels(panelB_display, fontsize=9, rotation=0, ha='center')
ax2.set_ylabel('Cosine distance', fontsize=10)
ax2.set_ylim(ylim_b)
ax2.set_title('(b) Cosine distance: NORA & reference VLMs', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold', loc='left')
ax2.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax2.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax2.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=9)
ax2.tick_params(axis='x', pad=8)
ax2.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.2, linewidth=0.5)
ax2.legend(loc='upper right', ncol=4, fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9,
           edgecolor='gray', handlelength=0.8, handletextpad=0.2, columnspacing=0.4)

plt.tight_layout(pad=0.5)
plt.subplots_adjust(bottom=0.15, wspace=0.3)

# ── Save ──
_REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
out_dir = os.path.join(_REPO_ROOT, 'docs', 'paper', 'figures')
art_dir = os.path.join(_REPO_ROOT, 'artifacts', 'figures', 'paper')

for d in [out_dir, art_dir]:
    os.makedirs(d, exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(f'{d}/fig_counterfactual_bar.pdf', dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
    fig.savefig(f'{d}/fig_counterfactual_bar.png', dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.close()
print('Done.')

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Plot dose-response ablation curve (Figure 7, right panel).

Shows Cohen's d (action MSE divergence) as a function of the number of
instruction-routing heads ablated, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

Output: fig_dose_response.pdf -> docs/paper/figures/ and artifacts/figures/paper/
"""
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')

# ── Font: Liberation Serif (metrically identical to Times New Roman) ──
matplotlib.rcParams['font.family'] = 'serif'
matplotlib.rcParams['font.serif'] = ['Liberation Serif', 'DejaVu Serif']
matplotlib.rcParams['mathtext.fontset'] = 'custom'
matplotlib.rcParams['mathtext.rm'] = 'Liberation Serif'
matplotlib.rcParams['mathtext.it'] = 'Liberation Serif:italic'
matplotlib.rcParams['mathtext.bf'] = 'Liberation Serif:bold'
matplotlib.rcParams['pdf.fonttype'] = 42
matplotlib.rcParams['ps.fonttype'] = 42

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import os

plt.rcParams.update({
    'font.size': 11,
    'axes.titlesize': 13,
    'axes.labelsize': 12,
    'xtick.labelsize': 10,
    'ytick.labelsize': 10,
    'legend.fontsize': 10,
    'figure.dpi': 300,
    'savefig.dpi': 300,
    'savefig.bbox': 'tight',
    'savefig.pad_inches': 0.05,
    'axes.spines.top': False,
    'axes.spines.right': False,
})

# ── Data ──
dose_n_heads = np.array([4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32])

dose_cohen_d = np.array([
    0.4815412850770599, 0.5082040281351017, 0.5600389203470800,
    0.5916585965181512, 0.5929310917614178, 0.6106991692401877,
    0.6192428662864000, 0.6385059409290664
])

dose_ci_lower = np.array([
    0.4493981998904407, 0.4792767313857140, 0.5292064204814684,
    0.5593699517760848, 0.5591344210287796, 0.5784721762082760,
    0.5866794567732834, 0.6033325798526022
])

dose_ci_upper = np.array([
    0.5111655435414341, 0.5407791509767693, 0.5928744039295671,
    0.6253230923848914, 0.6273837044447675, 0.6453009849211714,
    0.6538126323060768, 0.6711688584188803
])

ref_control_d = 0.41

# ── Plot ──
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.25, 2.6))

C_MAIN = '#1f77b4'
C_CTRL = '#d62728'
C_REGION = '#999999'

ax.fill_between(dose_n_heads, dose_ci_lower, dose_ci_upper,
                color=C_MAIN, alpha=0.15, edgecolor='none', zorder=2)

ax.plot(dose_n_heads, dose_cohen_d,
        '-o', color=C_MAIN, markersize=4.5, linewidth=1.4, zorder=3)

ax.axhline(ref_control_d, color=C_CTRL, linestyle='--', linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.5, zorder=1)
ax.text(33, 0.415, 'Control (8 random): $d$ = 0.41',
        fontsize=6.5, color=C_CTRL, ha='right', va='bottom')

for xb in [13, 20]:
    ax.axvline(xb, color=C_REGION, linestyle=':', linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.25, zorder=1)

y_lab = 0.72
ax.text(8, y_lab, 'Steep rise', fontsize=7, ha='center', color=C_REGION, style='italic')
ax.text(16.5, y_lab, 'Plateau', fontsize=7, ha='center', color=C_REGION, style='italic')
ax.text(27, y_lab, 'Slow rise', fontsize=7, ha='center', color=C_REGION, style='italic')

ax.set_xlabel('Number of heads ablated')
ax.set_ylabel("Cohen's $d$ (action MSE)")
ax.set_xticks(dose_n_heads)
ax.set_xlim(2, 34)
ax.set_ylim(0.35, 0.76)
ax.tick_params(direction='out', length=3)

plt.tight_layout()

# ── Save to both output directories ──
_REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
out_dirs = [
    os.path.join(_REPO_ROOT, 'docs', 'paper', 'figures'),
    os.path.join(_REPO_ROOT, 'artifacts', 'figures', 'paper'),
]
for d in out_dirs:
    os.makedirs(d, exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, 'fig_dose_response.pdf'), dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, 'fig_dose_response.png'), dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
    print(f"Saved: {d}/fig_dose_response.pdf/.png")

plt.close()

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

\looseness=-1
We presented a cross-architecture representational analysis of instruction routing in vision-language-action models, studying three VLAs built on distinct backbone families across four LIBERO task suites.
Our three complementary analyses---layer-wise action probing, counterfactual instruction perturbation, and L1 attention profiling---consistently decompose VLA instruction routing into two distinct patterns: training-associated effects and inherited base-model priors.
Exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.16$--$0.46$) and graded counterfactual sensitivity ($d = 0.45$--$1.52$) emerge specifically from VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning---absent in both VLA-to-VLA and NLP-only controls---while L1 attention routing is inherited from reference backbones.
These findings enable practical diagnostics: $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ flags under-utilized exit-layer representations without rollouts, and mid-layer features offer principled tap points for downstream reward models and planners.
The cross-architecture consistency---with mid-layer action-probe peaks converging to within $R^2 = 0.003$ despite divergent reference profiles---suggests these are general properties of autoregressive VLA fine-tuning, not artifacts of any single model design.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\looseness=-1
Our conclusions rest on $N{=}2$ VLM-to-VLA transitions plus one VLA-to-VLA case, all autoregressive decoders evaluated on a single benchmark (LIBERO); flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} action heads may behave differently.
All findings are correlational---$R^2$ measures decodability, not causal reliance---and evaluations are open-loop; the $\Delta R^2$--success-rate correlation ($\rho{=}0.583$, $p{=}0.10$; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}) is suggestive but underpowered ($n{=}9$).
Extending to additional architectures, non-autoregressive action heads, and closed-loop behavioral validation are priorities for future work.

1	"""Strip plot of ΔR² across four training pathway categories.
2	Shows that exit collapse emerges at VLM→VLA transition and does not intensify at VLA→VLA.
3	"""
4	import matplotlib
5	matplotlib.use("Agg")
6	import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
7	plt.rcParams.update({
8	    'font.family': 'serif',
9	    'font.serif': ['Liberation Serif'],
10	    'pdf.fonttype': 42,
11	    'ps.fonttype': 42,
12	    'mathtext.fontset': 'custom',
13	    'mathtext.rm': 'Liberation Serif',
14	    'mathtext.it': 'Liberation Serif:italic',
15	    'mathtext.bf': 'Liberation Serif:bold',
16	})
17	import numpy as np
18	import os
19	
20	# --- Data from Table 1 ---
21	categories = ["NLP\nfinetune", "Reference\n(pretrained)", "VLA→VLA\ntrained", "VLM→VLA\ntrained"]
22	
23	data = {
24	    "NLP\nfinetune": [
25	        (0.000, "Llama-2-chat"),
26	        (0.000, "Phi-3-instruct"),
27	        (0.000, "Qwen2.5-Instruct"),
28	    ],
29	    "Reference\n(pretrained)": [
30	        (0.065, "TraceVLA"),   # Goal ref
31	        (0.048, "TraceVLA"),   # Spatial ref
32	        (0.009, "TraceVLA"),   # Object ref
33	        (0.097, "TraceVLA"),   # Long ref
34	        (0.081, "NORA"),      # Goal ref
35	        (0.089, "NORA"),      # Spatial ref
36	        (0.056, "OpenVLA"),   # Goal ref
37	        (0.044, "OpenVLA"),   # Spatial ref
38	        (0.051, "OpenVLA"),   # Object ref
39	        (0.035, "OpenVLA"),   # Long ref
40	    ],
41	    "VLA→VLA\ntrained": [
42	        (0.086, "OpenVLA"),   # Goal
43	        (0.037, "OpenVLA"),   # Spatial
44	        (0.037, "OpenVLA"),   # Object
45	        (0.033, "OpenVLA"),   # Long
46	    ],
47	    "VLM→VLA\ntrained": [
48	        (0.333, "TraceVLA"),   # Goal
49	        (0.156, "TraceVLA"),   # Spatial
50	        (0.362, "TraceVLA"),   # Object
51	        (0.358, "TraceVLA"),   # Long
52	        (0.455, "NORA"),      # Goal
53	        (0.308, "NORA"),      # Spatial
54	    ],
55	}
56	
57	arch_markers = {"OpenVLA": "o", "TraceVLA": "s", "NORA": "D",
58	                "Llama-2-chat": "o", "Phi-3-instruct": "s", "Qwen2.5-Instruct": "D"}
59	arch_colors = {"OpenVLA": "#1f77b4", "TraceVLA": "#ff7f0e", "NORA": "#2ca02c",
60	               "Llama-2-chat": "#1f77b4", "Phi-3-instruct": "#ff7f0e", "Qwen2.5-Instruct": "#2ca02c"}
61	
62	fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 3.2))
63	
64	np.random.seed(42)
65	for i, cat in enumerate(categories):
66	    points = data[cat]
67	    for val, arch in points:
68	        jitter = np.random.uniform(-0.12, 0.12)
69	        ax.scatter(i + jitter, val, marker=arch_markers[arch], c=arch_colors[arch],
70	                   s=45, edgecolors="k", linewidths=0.4, zorder=3)
71

"""Strip plot of ΔR² across four training pathway categories.
Shows that exit collapse emerges at VLM→VLA transition and does not intensify at VLA→VLA.
"""
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    'font.family': 'serif',
    'font.serif': ['Liberation Serif'],
    'pdf.fonttype': 42,
    'ps.fonttype': 42,
    'mathtext.fontset': 'custom',
    'mathtext.rm': 'Liberation Serif',
    'mathtext.it': 'Liberation Serif:italic',
    'mathtext.bf': 'Liberation Serif:bold',
})
import numpy as np
import os

# --- Data from Table 1 ---
categories = ["NLP\nfinetune", "Reference\n(pretrained)", "VLA→VLA\ntrained", "VLM→VLA\ntrained"]

data = {
    "NLP\nfinetune": [
        (0.000, "Llama-2-chat"),
        (0.000, "Phi-3-instruct"),
        (0.000, "Qwen2.5-Instruct"),
    ],
    "Reference\n(pretrained)": [
        (0.065, "TraceVLA"),   # Goal ref
        (0.048, "TraceVLA"),   # Spatial ref
        (0.009, "TraceVLA"),   # Object ref
        (0.097, "TraceVLA"),   # Long ref
        (0.081, "NORA"),      # Goal ref
        (0.089, "NORA"),      # Spatial ref
        (0.056, "OpenVLA"),   # Goal ref
        (0.044, "OpenVLA"),   # Spatial ref
        (0.051, "OpenVLA"),   # Object ref
        (0.035, "OpenVLA"),   # Long ref
    ],
    "VLA→VLA\ntrained": [
        (0.086, "OpenVLA"),   # Goal
        (0.037, "OpenVLA"),   # Spatial
        (0.037, "OpenVLA"),   # Object
        (0.033, "OpenVLA"),   # Long
    ],
    "VLM→VLA\ntrained": [
        (0.333, "TraceVLA"),   # Goal
        (0.156, "TraceVLA"),   # Spatial
        (0.362, "TraceVLA"),   # Object
        (0.358, "TraceVLA"),   # Long
        (0.455, "NORA"),      # Goal
        (0.308, "NORA"),      # Spatial
    ],
}

arch_markers = {"OpenVLA": "o", "TraceVLA": "s", "NORA": "D",
                "Llama-2-chat": "o", "Phi-3-instruct": "s", "Qwen2.5-Instruct": "D"}
arch_colors = {"OpenVLA": "#1f77b4", "TraceVLA": "#ff7f0e", "NORA": "#2ca02c",
               "Llama-2-chat": "#1f77b4", "Phi-3-instruct": "#ff7f0e", "Qwen2.5-Instruct": "#2ca02c"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 3.2))

np.random.seed(42)
for i, cat in enumerate(categories):
    points = data[cat]
    for val, arch in points:
        jitter = np.random.uniform(-0.12, 0.12)
        ax.scatter(i + jitter, val, marker=arch_markers[arch], c=arch_colors[arch],
                   s=45, edgecolors="k", linewidths=0.4, zorder=3)

ax.axhline(0.10, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, zorder=1, label=r"$\Delta R^2 = 0.10$ threshold")

ax.set_xticks(range(len(categories)))
ax.set_xticklabels(categories, fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\Delta R^2$ (peak $-$ exit)", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(categories) - 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 0.50)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=8)

# Legend for architectures
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
handles = [
    Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="w", markerfacecolor="#1f77b4", markeredgecolor="k",
           markeredgewidth=0.4, markersize=6, label="OpenVLA / Llama-2"),
    Line2D([0], [0], marker="s", color="w", markerfacecolor="#ff7f0e", markeredgecolor="k",
           markeredgewidth=0.4, markersize=6, label="TraceVLA / Phi-3"),
    Line2D([0], [0], marker="D", color="w", markerfacecolor="#2ca02c", markeredgecolor="k",
           markeredgewidth=0.4, markersize=6, label="NORA / Qwen2.5"),
    Line2D([0], [0], color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, label=r"$\Delta R^2=0.10$"),
]
ax.legend(handles=handles, fontsize=6.5, loc="upper left", framealpha=0.9)

ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)

plt.tight_layout()

out_paper = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "docs", "paper", "figures", "fig_training_dynamics.pdf")
out_artifact = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "artifacts", "figures", "paper", "fig_training_dynamics.pdf")
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(out_paper), exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(out_artifact), exist_ok=True)
fig.savefig(out_paper, bbox_inches="tight", dpi=300)
fig.savefig(out_artifact, bbox_inches="tight", dpi=300)
print(f"Saved: {out_paper}")
print(f"Saved: {out_artifact}")
plt.close()

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    'font.family': 'serif',
    'font.serif': ['Liberation Serif'],
    'pdf.fonttype': 42,

    'mathtext.rm': 'Liberation Serif',
    'mathtext.it': 'Liberation Serif:italic',
    'mathtext.bf': 'Liberation Serif:bold',
})
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
import os

rows = [
    {
        'finding': 'Training-Associated\nExit Collapse',
        'description': '$R^2$ drops at exit layers\nafter VLA fine-tuning',
        'evidence': '6/6 VLM→VLA conditions\nshow Δ > 0.10;\n0/4 VLA→VLA;\n0/10 reference conditions',
        'limitation': 'Correlational,\nnot causal',
        'color': '#FDEBD0',
        'edge': '#E8A838',
    },
    {
        'finding': 'Action-Relevant\nSensitivity',
        'description': 'Counterfactual perturbation\nreveals action-linked\nrepresentations',
        'evidence': "Cohen's $d$ ≥ 0.45 across\n8 trained conditions;\nempty ranks first in 6/8",
        'limitation': '$d$ vs cosine metric\nincomparability',
        'color': '#D5F5E3',
        'edge': '#52BE80',
    },
    {
        'finding': 'Inherited Instruction\nAttention Prior',
        'description': 'L1 attention patterns\ninherited from\npre-trained VLMs',
        'evidence': 'Reference VLMs already\nshow task-structured\nattention',
        'limitation': 'Not causally\ntested',
        'color': '#D6EAF8',
        'edge': '#5DADE2',
    },
]

col_labels = ['Finding', 'Evidence', 'Limitation']
col_colors = ['#2C3E50', '#2C3E50', '#2C3E50']

fig_w, fig_h = 7.0, 3.2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(fig_w, fig_h))
ax.set_xlim(0, fig_w)
ax.set_ylim(0, fig_h)
ax.axis('off')

box_h = 0.72
row_gap = 0.18
top_y = fig_h - 0.55

col_x = [0.15, 1.65, 3.35, 5.55]
col_w = [1.35, 1.55, 2.05, 1.25]

header_y = top_y + 0.10
header_labels = ['Finding', '', 'Evidence', 'Limitation']
for ci in [0, 2, 3]:
    cx = col_x[ci] + col_w[ci] / 2
    ax.text(cx, header_y, header_labels[ci], ha='center', va='bottom',
            fontsize=11, fontweight='bold', color='#2C3E50')

for ri, row in enumerate(rows):
    y_center = top_y - ri * (box_h + row_gap) - box_h / 2

    for ci, (key, x, w) in enumerate(zip(
        ['finding', 'description', 'evidence', 'limitation'],
        col_x, col_w
    )):
        if ci == 0:
            fc = row['color']
            ec = row['edge']
            fw = 'bold'
            fs = 9
        elif ci == 1:
            fc = '#FAFAFA'
            ec = '#CCCCCC'
            fw = 'normal'
            fs = 8
        elif ci == 2:
            fc = '#F0F7FC'
            ec = '#85C1E9'
            fw = 'normal'
            fs = 8
        else:
            fc = '#FDF2F2'
            ec = '#E6A0A0'
            fw = 'normal'
            fs = 8

        rect = mpatches.FancyBboxPatch(
            (x, y_center - box_h / 2), w, box_h,
            boxstyle='round,pad=0.06',
            facecolor=fc, edgecolor=ec, linewidth=1.2
        )
        ax.add_patch(rect)
        ax.text(x + w / 2, y_center, row[key],
                ha='center', va='center', fontsize=fs, fontweight=fw,
                color='#333333', linespacing=1.3)

    for ci in range(3):
        x_start = col_x[ci] + col_w[ci] + 0.02
        x_end = col_x[ci + 1] - 0.02
        ax.annotate('', xy=(x_end, y_center), xytext=(x_start, y_center),
                     arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#888888',
                                     lw=1.5, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))

plt.tight_layout(pad=0.2)

_REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
out_dirs = [
    os.path.join(_REPO_ROOT, 'docs', 'paper', 'figures'),
    os.path.join(_REPO_ROOT, 'artifacts', 'figures', 'paper'),
]
for d in out_dirs:
    os.makedirs(d, exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, 'fig_claim_evidence.pdf'), dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, 'fig_claim_evidence.png'), dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')

plt.close()
print('Saved fig_claim_evidence.')
